utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you, and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So good morning to you all. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, together with Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: John Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin, Your Honour, and Tania Radosavljevic, my legal assistant, is with me. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Maitre Pitron with Mrs. Fauveau and Mr. Masson representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. May I have the case called now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I ask Your Honour to go into closed session for the next witness, may I raise the question of the timetable for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I am sorry I did not get back to you, but after -- I sorted it out almost immediately. But then it just -- I forgot all about it, and then remembered it about 6.00. But then I anticipated that no news usually would be good news. So no, no, we are not having a sitting on Friday afternoon. We are having the sitting tomorrow morning, as previously scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I discussed it with Judge Hunt, because we were sort of trying to accommodate each other, because he needs to sit with the other two Judges too, and we had a little bit of a problem. So we sorted it out. When I told him that you need to be in London, he said, "Ms. Korner comes first."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm tempted to say if I believe that, I'd believe anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Maitre Pitron, how is Maitre de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for this question. Mr. De Roux is very well. At the moment -- he's very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Give him our regards, and we wish him a quick recovery, and see him back here as quickly as possible. As early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did it again, Your Honour. I think you're just going to have to shoot me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't forget that we are going to be in closed session, Mr. Ackerman, today. It's not the first time that I have confiscated a mobile phone, Mr. Ackerman. The first time I did was quite a few years ago. Which reminds me. Mr. Ackerman, my attention has been drawn to the fact that the documents that you requested to have admitted as exhibits yesterday have, according to the registry, never been forwarded to the registry. Oh, they have? I see. They have never been tendered, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought that's what I did yesterday when I offered them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, does that constitute a problem to you, Ms. Korner? Not really, I would imagine. But it's just a formality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm just asking to be reminded what the documents were. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. What was the content? That was all I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I have no idea at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know if we've seen them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've definitely seen them. They were given to everybody, way back at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: According to Ms. Gustin, who keeps track of this, we never saw BT47 and BT48. So it may be that copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, would you deal with it during the break, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next thing I had my attention drawn to this morning was the witness who we will be having before us today is BT7. And the registry is telling me that, previously, they have followed a different system. Madam registrar, could you explain what you meant by what you told me this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Normally, the registry designates a letter of the alphabet, beginning with "A." We go through the complete alphabet, and then we begin with AB, AC, AD. It -- we find that it's easier for us to keep track, but not only that, when the judgement is being written, it's a little bit easier for the people to be able to follow the letters and the names correspondingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there's going -- I'm sorry. There's going to be a difficulty. The reason it's BT7 is because we numbered in our motions for protective measures and the like, and that's how they've been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I personally was unaware that there was this strict rule that you had to go A, B, C. And the reason, from previous experience, I said let's have BTs-1 through to whatever, is that you end up exactly as the registrar says, with double A's or double B's, and it gets, in my experience, even more confusing. I'm afraid the difficulty is though that if we now change the numbering, the motions aren't going to make any sense. And I'm not sure what the real difficulty is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can -- I think for the reasons stated by you, Ms. Korner, we can retain the present identification and then we'll see later on if it creates problems. We'll see how to go around it and find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we will certainly do is at the end of the Prosecution's case, we will provide Your Honours with a full list of the pseudonym witnesses and what the pseudonyms were. As I said, it's BT7 because they were numbered for the protective measure motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's correct. I think -- is there anything else? Oh, there is something else I wanted to raise myself. Mr. Ackerman, could I possibly ask you to be kind enough during the weekend to prepare a very short motion asking for -- formally asking, requesting, what you asked for yesterday, that is, for the documents which are in possession of Witness Dzonlic, sort of identifying exactly which documents you need, so that we can then work on it immediately. In other words, we have started working on it already, but we have come to the conclusion that it is better to have a proper motion from you, rather than the way you addressed it yesterday. So that we will give the -- even the Prosecution an opportunity to respond to it if you want to, either -- either orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll get it to you as quick as I can, maybe even tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Something very short, very concise, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we expressed our position yesterday. But I'll double-check that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I am doing this, I don't know, because something told me take an extra precaution in case the witness himself decides to make representations. So that way we will all be properly hedged in. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's a problem. The problem arose from our side rather than his. He was willing to hand over his files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. So we can bring the witness in. Where is the usher? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will go -- we will go into closed session. And I appeal to you to be careful in not addressing the witness by his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, like Your Honour, this is my first experience for closed session, so it's going to -- it's likely to lead to some trouble on my part. Your Honour, I understand the system is that he's shown the piece of paper which I've handed to the registrar, just asked to identify him, and it's shown to the Defence. And Your Honours, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have taken the trouble to ask for a video recording of some closed sessions before to see how it goes. I mean, otherwise, you just address the witness as Mr. Witness and -- or "Witness."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm hoping to get away with calling him "sir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or "sir" or whatever. But previously, he's always been addressed as "witness," "witness," "witness."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I've seen it myself. But I just think it sounds so odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends. Because if he's familiar with the English, he might aspire for the knighthood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Make certain, Your Honour that, when he is handed the piece of paper to read his name, that he's carefully instructed to read it silently, because on occasion they have read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
